newsitem.title: GERMANY: Yeltsin, Kohl set for tough talk in Baden-Baden.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin, Kohl set for tough talk in Baden-Baden.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin will get a warm welcome on Thursday from Chancellor Helmut Kohl, his best friend in the West, but he also faces some tough talking on NATO expansion.

On the eve of the talks in the stately spa Of Baden-Baden, Yeltsin's spokesman had harsh words for NATO, warning Moscow would reject a treaty that is in the works if it did not guarantee the alliance would not move troops and arms eastwards.
Kohl's requests for the return of priceless artworks, seized by the Red Army from Nazi Germany, could also spoil the two leaders' digestion during a long working lunch.
Kremlin spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky warned that Russia would demand its price and push its claims on property in Germany.
A silent and serious Yeltsin flew in to Stuttgart on Wednesday for a visit built around his acceptance on Thursday evening of a "Man of the Year" award from the German media.

He will spend the day in a tete-a-tete with Kohl, strolling in brilliant spring sunshine in the gardens of Baden-Baden, home to a casino immortalised by Dostoyevsky and to grand hotels that once hosted kings, tsars and emperors.

The two leaders will meet at 11.15 am (0915 GMT) in the $2,000-a-night Brenner's Park Hotel, surrounded by tight security and flying the Russian tricolour in honour of Yeltsin's stay. He spent the evening preparing for the talks.
The focus of the talks will be a working lunch in a country restaurant followed by a planned walk in a vineyard.

Through all the criticism Yeltsin has suffered and through his serious illness last year, his most constant supporter in the West has been Helmut Kohl. Yastrzhembsky said he was now hoping for Kohl's help in reaching a compromise with NATO.
But the tone of his media briefing ahead of the second meeting with Kohl in just over three months had a hard edge.

Yeltsin is to brief Kohl on his Helsinki summit last month with U.S. President Bill Clinton, which laid the groundwork for efforts to draw up a treaty or "charter" between Russia and NATO that would give Moscow some say in the alliance after it extends membership to some former Soviet bloc states.

But, Yastrzhembsky said, the signing of a treaty was by no means a foregone conclusion and the expansion of NATO into eastern Europe remained, in Moscow's view, "the West's biggest historic mistake since the end of the Cold War".
"Without binding and concrete terms in the treaty on military issues, there would scarcely be any point in Russia signing such a document," Yastrzhembsky said.
It was "premature" to forecast the chances of a treaty being signed at the end of May, as had been hoped.

Russia has made it clear it does not want Western troops and weapons moving closer to its borders. NATO, however, does not want new members -- set to be invited to join in July -- to lack the defence guarantees of existing partners.

Yeltsin, who is visiting with his wife Naina and, for the first time in such a public role abroad, his younger daughter Tatyana Dyachenko, has brought a valuable piece of treasure for Kohl, Yastrzhembsky said. He declined to say what it was.
Russia's hoard of German art has long been a bone of contention and has not helped Moscow's urgings -- to be repeated in Baden-Baden -- that Germany invest more in Russia.

Yastrzhembsky said Yeltsin was very keen on Kohl's proposal for a joint world-wide exhibition tour of the best captured art. But, he added, Germany's Western allies like Britain and the United States, who also hold art seized from the Nazis, should also be asked to join in.

Yeltsin, in turn, would ask Kohl to return property to the Russian Orthodox Church -- including the onion-domed church in Baden-Baden. Hitler handed the property to the church formed by Russian exiles who fled the Bolshevik revolution.

Moscow wanted recognition for having sent back much of the captured art, mostly to former East Germany, and of the huge cultural damage inflicted on Russia by the Nazi invasion. Yastrzhembsky suggested Bonn might pay for some pieces.

Promising that Yeltsin would counter the "hysterics" of Russia's communist-led parliament, which is trying to block any return of the disputed artworks, Yastrzhembsky said the two leaders would work for a solution. But it would take time.
